title: Expressions and operators (arithmetic, logic, null handling)
hook: Operators turn values into expressions. The ones you will use most in production are null-coalescing (??) and null-conditional (?.) — they keep cache lookups and token payloads from throwing. C# 14 adds null-conditional assignment so ?. can appear on the left of =.

blocks.text: An **expression** is code that produces a value: `5 + 3` evaluates to `8`. An **operator** is the symbol that performs the action: `+`, `==`, `&&`, `??`. C# operators follow a **precedence** order (multiplication before addition, for example). When in doubt, use parentheses. Unlike JavaScript, C# does not coerce types in comparisons — `==` on two strings compares content, and comparing a string to a number is a compile error.

entries.plainDefinition: Returns the left value if it is not null; otherwise returns the right value.
entries.example: string json = cached ?? "{}"; — uses "{}" when cached is null.

entries.plainDefinition: Accesses a member only when the receiver is not null; otherwise the whole expression is null.
entries.example: int? ttl = cacheEntry?.TtlSeconds; — null if cacheEntry is null.

entries.plainDefinition: Logical operators (&& and ||) stop evaluating as soon as the result is known.
entries.example: if (user != null && user.IsActive) — IsActive is never called when user is null.

blocks.text: Integer division truncates toward zero: `5 / 2` is `2`, not `2.5`. Use `decimal` or `double` when you mean real division. Short-circuit logical operators (`&&`, `||`) skip the right side when the answer is already decided — critical when the right side would throw on a null reference. The null-coalescing operator (`??`) and null-conditional operator (`?.`) are your first line of defense against NullReferenceException in service code.

blocks.title: C# 14 null-conditional assignment
blocks.body: Before C# 14 you wrote if (msg is not null) msg.RetryCount = n;. Now msg?.RetryCount = n; is legal. The right-hand side runs only when the receiver is not null. Do not confuse this with ??=, which assigns when the left value is already null.

items.title: Parentheses first
items.body: Anything inside ( ) is evaluated before anything outside.

items.title: Logical and null-coalescing
items.body: && and || short-circuit. ?? sits lower — parenthesize when mixing ?? with ?:.

diagram.title: Null-safe access flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Evaluate receiver] --> B{Is receiver null?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Skip member access — result is null]
  B -->|No| D[Access member or assign value]
  D --> E[Return result]

sections.heading: Code walkthrough: arithmetic and null operators

snippet.label: Arithmetic and comparison basics
snippet.explanation: Integer / truncates toward zero. string == compares content. && stops evaluating when the left side is false.

snippet.label: Null-coalescing and null-conditional
snippet.explanation: ?? supplies a fallback when the left side is null. ?. skips member access when the receiver is null. Null-conditional assignment (C# 14) does not evaluate the right-hand side when the receiver is null.

snippet.label: ??= versus ?. =
snippet.explanation: ??= assigns when the variable is null. ?. = skips the entire right-hand side when the receiver is null — important when the RHS hits a database or deserializes a token.

blocks.title: C# vs JavaScript/TypeScript operators
rows: JS == coerces types; TS uses === for strict

blocks.title: Top pitfalls
blocks.body: Using == on floating-point for money — use decimal and exact compares. Writing x ?? y ?? z then mixing with ?: without parentheses. Assuming customer?.Order = GetOrder() always calls GetOrder() — it does not when customer is null. Using & and | on bool when you meant && and || — the non-short-circuit versions evaluate both sides.

interviewTakeaways: Integer division truncates; use decimal or double when you mean real division.
&& and || short-circuit; & and | on bool do not.
C# 14: x?.Prop = expr assigns only if x is not null; the right-hand side is skipped otherwise.
??= assigns when the left is null; ?. = assigns when the receiver is not null — different conditions.
commonPitfalls: Using == on floating point for money — use decimal and exact compares, or a tolerance for double.
Writing x ?? y ?? z then mixing with ?: without parentheses.
Assuming customer?.Order = GetOrder() always calls GetOrder() — it does not when customer is null.
Confusing ??= (assign if null) with ?. = (assign if receiver is not null).

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has ?? and ?. but optional chaining on the left of assignment is a syntax error. C# 14 allows x?.Prop = v. JavaScript == coerces types; C# == does not.
